summary: The listener is built to admire Roland, dread the ambush he will not call for help against, grieve his death, and savor Ganelon's punishment.

need-to-breathe.why: Nothing is built to affect the listener's breath.

hungry.why: Nothing is built to produce hunger.

full.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

thirsty.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

gassy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

need-to-poop.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

need-to-pee.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

sleepy.why: A sung epic does not aim to lull its hearers.

nauseous.why: Nothing is built to sicken the listener.

urge-to-sneeze.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

urge-to-cough.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

dizzy.why: Nothing is built to produce vertigo.

fatigued.why: The listener is not made to feel bodily exertion.

pain.why: Brains spilling from split helms and Roland's bursting temples are built to make the listener wince.

disgusted.why: The monstrous pagan tribes are built to repel, mildly.

itchy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

tickled.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

over-stimulated.why: Nothing is built to overwhelm the senses.

too-hot-too-cold.why: Nothing is built to make the listener feel heat or cold.

afraid.why: The hundred thousand pagans massing in the pass are built to frighten on the rearguard's behalf.

anxious.why: The listener, told the ambush is coming, dreads it through every laisse of the approach.

panic.why: Nothing is built to produce panic in the listener.

sensory-pleasures.why: Nothing is built to give the listener sensory pleasure.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: The assonanced laisses, the repeated laisses similaires, and the formulaic grandeur are built for a listening audience's pleasure.

piquancy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

fun-excitement.why: The clash of the twelve peers against the pagan kings and Charlemagne's duel with Baligant are built as thrilling spectacle.

orgasm.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

love-romantic.why: Aude's death at the news of Roland is built for a single pang.

love-family.why: Charlemagne's grief for his nephew is built to touch the listener as a parent's.

grief.why: Roland's death facing Spain, Charlemagne tearing his beard, and the funeral at Blaye are built to produce mourning.

missing-someone.why: Charlemagne's lament for his lost right arm gives a moment of felt absence.

aroused-sexually.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

liking-as-a-friend.why: The listener is built to love Roland and Oliver as a pair and feel their reconciliation at Oliver's death.

empathy.why: The listener shares Roland's dying regret and Charlemagne's weariness, but the pagans are given little interior.

compassion.why: The slaughter of the rearguard and the aged emperor's tears are built to produce pity.

grateful.why: Nothing is built to make the listener grateful.

pleasure-from-helping.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

trustful-distrustful.why: The listener watches Ganelon plot with Marsile while Charlemagne trusts him, a dramatic irony that breeds suspicion.

depressed.why: Nothing is built to make the listener feel unsupported.

angry.why: Ganelon's treachery is built to anger the listener from the moment it is sworn.

envious.why: Nothing is built to produce envy.

jealous-romantic-sexual.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

jealous-friendship.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

hatred.why: The poem is built to make a Christian audience hate the pagans and Ganelon; pagans are wrong, Christians are right.

contempt.why: Ganelon's self-serving defense and the pagans' flight are built to draw scorn.

resentment.why: The listener feels the outrage of a betrayed rearguard and of a court that nearly lets the traitor go.

proud.why: Sweet France and Charlemagne's majesty are built to swell a French listener's pride.

amused.why: Roland's laugh at Ganelon and the old men's chess are the poem's scant lightness.

sense-of-belonging.why: The poem recruits the listener to Christian France against the pagans; its coalitional pull is its purpose.

lonely.why: Roland alone on the field after every companion has fallen gives the listener a moment of isolation.

judgy-moral-sense.why: The listener is made judge of Roland's pride, Ganelon's treason, and the barons' cowardly verdict before God decides.

admiration.why: The poem is built to make the listener admire Roland's valor, Oliver's wisdom, Turpin's zeal, and Charlemagne's majesty.

embarrassed.why: Ganelon dropping the glove gives a flicker of secondhand embarrassment.

shame.why: The listener feels Roland's fear of a shameful song but is not shamed.

guilt.why: Nothing is built to make the listener guilty.

sad.why: The deaths of the peers, Roland's farewell to Durendal, and Charlemagne's tears are built for sorrow.

happy.why: Nothing is built to make the listener content.

joyful-euphoric.why: Charlemagne's victory over Baligant gives a surge of triumph.

effort.why: The repetitive laisses and the long Baligant episode ask persistence of a reader, less of a listener.

focused-in-flow.why: The horn debate and the battle at Roncevaux are built to hold attention tightly.

bored.why: The Baligant battle's catalogues can tire a reader, though not by design.

impatient.why: The three refusals of the horn are built to make the listener strain for Roland to blow it.

curious.why: The listener wants to know whether Charlemagne will arrive and how Ganelon will be judged.

surprised.why: Aude's instant death is the one event built to startle; the rest is foretold.

awe.why: The sun standing still, the portents over France, and the angels at Roland's death are built to produce awe.

skeptical-doubtful.why: The listener is given no cause to doubt the teller.

feeling-of-knowing.why: The repeated laisses let the listener recognize rather than recall.

confused.why: The laisses similaires retell moments with variations that can puzzle a modern reader, though not by design.

frustrated.why: Roland's refusal to blow the horn is built to frustrate the listener who sees what it will cost.

uncertain-certain.why: The outcome at Roncevaux is certain; only Ganelon's trial holds any doubt.

understanding.why: The listener understands the poem's law, that pride and treason both must be paid, as the trial closes it.

inspired.why: Roland's death may inspire a listener to valor; the poem is built to do so.

satisfied.why: Ganelon torn apart and his kinsmen hanged close the account, though Charlemagne's new summons leaves a remainder.

foreboding.why: The poet announces the betrayal before it happens and Charlemagne's dreams spell it out; the listener dreads Roncevaux from the first laisses.

nostalgia.why: The poem's longing for a heroic Christian past is built into its telling.

anticipation-suspense.why: Will Roland blow the horn, will Charlemagne hear it, will Thierry beat Pinabel: three suspenses the poem builds in turn.

hope.why: The listener hopes Charlemagne will arrive in time, a hope the poem builds and denies.

schadenfreude.why: Ganelon's quartering and the pagans drowning in the Ebro are built to be enjoyed.

elevation.why: Roland's death with his glove raised to God and Thierry's lone stand for justice are built to uplift.

infatuation.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

rage.why: Roland's fury after Oliver's death and Charlemagne's vengeful pursuit carry the listener along in rage.
